title: What the Science of Reading Says 'Post-Phonics' & Meeting Up in Nashville n-nashville/
author: Doug Lemov
summary: Doug Lemov previews a forthcoming book with Colleen Driggs and Erica Woolway that argues systematic synthetic phonics, while essential, is only the starting point of reading instruction -- not the whole story. He lays out seven research-backed arguments for what should happen in reading classrooms once students can decode: fluency is a prerequisite for comprehension at every grade level; once fluent, background knowledge (not a generic transferable 'skill') is the biggest driver of comprehension; vocabulary is the single most important form of knowledge, though often mistaught as a skill; attention is central to reading and must be deliberately built; writing in response to reading reinforces the same underlying code reading relies on; the ability to handle complex text gates long-term academic success; and books remain the optimal format for building deep understanding. Lemov frames the piece as the first in a series of excerpts from the book, alongside a plug for an in-person Reading Reconsidered workshop in Nashville.
points: Lemov's framing -- phonics is 'job one' but not the whole job -- directly challenges any reading-instruction model that stops at decoding and assumes comprehension will follow automatically once students can sound out words.

His second argument (background knowledge, not a generic transferable skill, drives comprehension) takes a direct stance in the ongoing 'skills vs. knowledge' debate in reading research, siding firmly with knowledge-building over generic strategy instruction.

The claim that vocabulary is 'often taught as if it were a skill' identifies a specific, common instructional mismatch: vocabulary is background knowledge and should be taught and acquired accordingly, not treated as a transferable technique.

Naming attention as 'central to every learning activity especially reading' and explicitly invoking the smartphone's effect on attention connects reading pedagogy to a broader contemporary concern about sustained focus.

Ranking books as the 'optimal text format' -- not just one option among digital alternatives -- makes a specific, testable claim about format, not just content, that will matter for schools weighing screen-based reading platforms.
quotes: The book describes seven key arguments that we think tell us what should happen in reading classrooms "post phonics," and we can probably best capture what we mean by that phrase with a diagram.
But… systematic synthetic phonics shouldn't be the only thing students do in the primary grades even if it's the most important.
Fluency is the ability to read words quickly and easily as soon as they are encountered.
Unfortunately there is little evidence that the skill translates and significant evidence that the skills happen naturally when readers have sufficient background knowledge to disambiguate texts.
Attention is the currency of learning-in almost any task. But reading, especially, relies on and requires states of sustained focus and concentration.
Books package information and ideas in a unique form to which our brains are especially receptive from a learning stand point.
The number of dysfluent students in your classroom is almost assuredly far higher than you think!
